projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Nicholas S. Vargo was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Nicholas S. Vargo. Mr. Vargo served in the U.S. Army Air Core with the 445th Bomb Group, 700th Squadron. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was Tech Sergeant. Nick was a Prisoner of War. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Vargo's home in Novelty, Ohio on June 22,2004. Nick was 83 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: It was Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: It was off 93th Street, off of Buckeye.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Not too much, I mean, I was rather young -- and didn't really sink in at that time. But we knew it had happened. I mean, we were all alerted to the fact -- we are probably going to go to war. I was just in the prime drafting year -- you know -- to be drafted. So we had that in the back of our minds. And we were just starting to enjoy life -- being young and getting your first car -- you know -- thinking of the girls at the time -- you know. So we didn't worry too much. Until we were actually drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, how old were you then, in '41 at that time?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Uh...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Out of school?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I was 21.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 21. Okay.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, did you have a job then? At that point?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yes. I -- I worked at Camera Hardware on Buckeye Road. I was managing the hardware store, and just local hardware and neighborhood store. And, I enjoyed the job. I loved working in a hardware store -- people come in wanting information on repairs and stuff. So it was a good job and -- and I was bilingual. I talked Hungarian, which was a Hungarian neighborhood. So the owner was well pleased with me because I could converse. Everybody would come in and want to talk to the Hungarian boy -- you know -- in Hungarian. So, I was an asset to his store which I -- I enjoyed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, when did you get your greetings from Uncle Sam?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, I was working there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: And -- let's see, when did I go in -- 1942.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: In September '42. And, we went ___ a few fellows from the neighborhood. And we went to Camp Perry which was a radical change in the way we lived. We happened to go in on a Friday night and they were serving liver, it was not like mama's cooking. And oh, we were like all down in the dumps being away from home for the first time -- so you were trying to accustom yourself to -- you know -- a new way of life. It was a good thing we had a lot of the neighborhood boys there -- I mean -- you were amongst friends there so it wasn't really that bad. And, of course, they keep you busy -- you know -- going here -- shots and getting into the old army swing. But, stayed there for a few days and then they transferred us to Atlantic City, and I said -- boy, if this is the army this is going to be great. Lived in apartments there, of course, they were stripped down, but it wasn't an army life. And, they want to know where you want to go, or what would you like to do. But, they were recruiting for the Air Force at the time, and that pleased me. I mean I -- hey -- right --this is exactly where I want to go. So, I signed up for -- for a mechanic -- you know -- I said 'well', and then they sent me to Lincoln, Nebraska. To single engine airplane mechanics. And went through a training there -- getting...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, I think, we were in Lincoln -- Lincoln, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea, Lincoln Nebraska. Went through school -- single engine fighters going to be Ypsilanti, Michigan, at the Ford Bomber Plant -- B-24s. So, here I am, Four Engine Manny (ph) after that. And, you're suppose to fly out of there a crew chief on a B-24, but I guess they had different ideas and I was sent to Arlington, Texas, gunnery school. Well, okay -- if you -- fine gunneries fine. So, went down there -- went through gunnery school and became an engineer gunner or flight engineer, which they called us. And left there -- let's see -- I think I, well anyway's (sic), I traveled around the West. I went to Clovis, New Mexico; Pablo. Up into Utah, Salt Lake City and finally we were put together with a crew and we ended up in Topeka, Kansas. So, we finally rounded out our crew -- ten members. And we were getting ready to be assigned to a squad -- a group that was going to the Pacific because they got suntans. And, apparently they got a urgent call for 25 crews to be sent to England. Well, we were one of the 25. And put us on the train, sent us up to Camp Shanks -- which we sat around there for about a month, and every night into New York City -- you know -- this is a great life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do for fun in New York City?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well -- you know -- went to shows, bars, and, so it was interesting -- you know. And, finally, we shipped out on the Queen Elizabeth and ended up in Scotland. And, we were assigned to the 445th Bomb Group, 700 Squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: And, this was in -- about December '43 we were there. And the highlight of the thing was Jimmy Stewart was a squadron commander. At the time he was only a captain. And I run across him one day going to the mess hall. And, I look at the guy and I say Jeez (ph) -- I know -- I know this fellow. And, he's got this day growth of beard and given the slope (ph) I never talked with him or anything -- but, I went by a bit later on -- I went -- hay that's Jimmy Stewart. And the guy says yea he's a squadron commander in 703. And, he stayed there for awhile, of course, he went on -- you know -- to higher up into the head group and into headquarters later on. But he -- he did 20 missions with us -- you know -- apparently I may have been been a few that he led too -- you know -- our squadron. Well, I -- I did about 15, and on our 16th mission we were going to Wickhow (ph), I think that's how you pronounce it. But, it -- it -- the day of the raid it seemed like -- boy this isn't going to be it. Take-off was postponed and we waited for another hour and then finally we got the take-off signal, the flare. And, we were going, and we were into Germany, and we got jumped by fighters. Well, the first sweep they came through the formation. Must have hit our ailerons, or anyways (sic) knocked us out of formation and we started going down. We were about 25,000 and he gives the bail out signal and the guys in back went out on the back first thing. And the radio man grabbed me by the leg and says, come on, I was in the top turret so, we get down on the -- in the bomb bay getting ready to jump. Well, the pilot and copilot still sitting there and they finally leveled out the ship. So, I looked at John, the radioman, we crawled back up to the deck. I got him back in -- into the turret. At that time there was two fighters coming in on us, apparently thinking we were dead. Well, I open up on them -- and at that time I considered a hit on both of them. But, I couldn't see them going down because I'm the top turret. So, I figured -- well, I don't know if I got them I -- don't know -- and that was the end of that. And finally Brocko (ph) pulled my leg. When I jumped out I disconnected all the intercom so I couldn't hear -- and he's grabbing me by the leg -- come on, let's go. And we get down to the bomb bay, we're getting ready to jump. Apparently, another fighter came up from underneath and give us a blast. Well, John got a direct hit right above the leg. And, I was right next to him and I picked up little shrapnel, but he hit the gas tank right above us and it was a big explosion and it blew me out of the airplane. I mean, I don't recall jumping -- the ship did explode. And, I got facial burns and, when I landed -- coming down I didn't know where we were -- Germany, or where, I had no information. But, I hit the ground -- I did a beautiful landing. As far as parachute jumping it was great. And I'm sitting on the ground -- now what do you do -- you know. So I see a young fellow coming at me with his hands in the air -- poof poof. What's this guy want? Well, he wanted to know if I had a gun. And, he comes up to me and hugs me. And I say, man what a greeting I'm getting down here -- you know. Here I was -- I was in Luxemburg and they --they were Belgium boys. So he grabs me and says come on, and we go to a shelter in the woods, in a ravine. Apparently, they were cutting wood or whatever there but, I met an older man, a young daughter and we kind of talked back and forth as best we can because they didn't understand me I didn't understand them. Then I had my escape kit in my knee and I pulled that out, and opened up the maps and said I well where am I, and she said -- you know -- Belgium. I said I want to go to France and into Spain. And, they said okay. Well, anyway the old man goes away -- and the girl -- they come back later. And with a complete civilian clothes. So they take all my flight clothes away and I'm dressed like a civilian -- you know. The gal kind of gives me first-aid on the -- on the face. And we're sitting there, they brought some tea over and we're trying to exchange -- tell them who I am, where I'm from, and... so. And while we were sitting there we hear something coming down one side of the ravine, and here it was a German out looking for us. So, we take off with the two Belgium boys and we were running down sort of in a ravine and he said while we'll going to the bottom and come back on the other side. Well, when we got down into the opening at the bottom there was another German patrol on the other ridge. And, well they give us a couple of shots -- and well -- that was it. I was -- we just froze -- you know -- and that's when I was captured. Of course, as soon as they got me I pulled out the old dog tags and I'm thinking -- boy, here I am in civilian clothes. And, couple of the good guards -- you know -- they kind of boot you around a little bit until the English speaking officer apparently came there and was telling me what are you doing in civilian clothes? I say well, I got burnt -- you know -- I got burnt and I found them on a clothes line. Okay, so they take me up and put me in with civilians. Must have been the Gestapo or SS whichever. Sort of a little convertible like car, anyway they drive me up to a farmhouse. I was standing there, little old man come up to me and he's waving a fist in my face -- you know -- I don't understand what he is saying. So, later I realize they must have said that he gave me the clothes -- you know. They were trying to figure out who it was. Well, to me he was totally unknown -- you know. Well, from there I left and I went to -- they put me in a jail cell, and they interrogated me. And then, I think, I went to two different prisons -- like, and then one day they take me into this stockade, it was like a -- a youth camp, or a school. It was -- and into the guardhouse and I was standing there and these little kids come out with their little pants -- you know -- in the morning and they raised the flag. So, in the guardhouse there was a sergeant there that spoke English and he give me first-aid on the face, bandaged me up. And apparently the news spread in the camp, or the compound, that they had an American. And, these little kids they would all come by, by the window. And I --I figured they were coming to look at me so I purposely stood by the window -- you know. And, they'd all come staring at me as I was there. And, from there they sent me up to Belgium to a hospital. And, that's where I -- I run into Brocko, and they amputated his leg there and he went somewhere else -- and our copilot was there. He had a broken leg. He said when the ship was burning he drove out from the flight deck and he hit his leg and... so, I didn't see the pilot or anybody. And, the navigator and bombardier they all were somewhere else -- you know. Apparently, as we bailed out at different times so we lost one another. But, I was the only enlisted man caught. The four in the back never were captured.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, they were able to get away?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yes. They -- they stayed with the resistance and they stayed in Belgium until the Americans finally came after D-Day. About five month they were back, but they were never -- never captured. And I was sent to a prison camp -- well, up to Frankford, interrogation center. And, they constantly wanted to know where I got the clothes, and I stayed maybe a week or so in solitary confinement. And, after they were though with me they put you in a little camp right next door to the interrogation center where they'd keep you to send you to a prison camp. Well, anyway I was in civilian clothes -- you know -- I went in the compound it happened to be my good friend later on, Norm Rustle, was in the camp at the time and he says -- who is this guy coming here? You think the Germans would be that dumb to put a guy in civilian clothes so, but nobody would talk to me I mean, I was -- I didn't know anybody. But, finally we were sent up to Stalag 4-- up close to Dychow and about 56 of us open up a brand new camp -- with no food, not much of a shelter there. And, we stayed there for a few months, and we had a -- when the Russians evacuated another prison camp they brought them up to our camp. They had the young marines bringing them in, and when they ran from the station to the camp they double-timed them. And, they put the dogs on them, and the bayoneting them as ran up there, which was the highlight of one of the things. Another one was, there was a German working on a pole and he was electrocuted, and, of course, we kind of were happy to see this happen -- which is -- probably wasn't right -- you know -- the poor guy. But, then the Germans run us all into the barracks and that said they would shoot us all if we don't keep quiet. But, that was one of the incidents in the camp. And, then -- well, from there when the Germans, rather the Russians came closer they evacuated the camp. And, they put us in a boxcar -- they filled it up pretty good. And, we went out -- and they -- going through Berlin they left us -- left us on a siding and the British come in that night and was bombing and here we were locked up in a -- in a -- boxcar. And, I says, boy, one of those guys is going to drop one right on our head. Then we moved out of there and went into Nuremberg and we stayed there for a little while. But, that was an another good place where the British would come in at night and bomb and those barracks would when they dropped a bomb would just bounce off the ground they were just on foundations -- and a couple of guys were ready to -- you know -- call it quits or something from the bombing. But, it was a camp with a lot of Russians in there. They would take them out there during the day to -- on work details and they would bring them back at night, and man, they would be beat-up and whatnot. But, that was where I got a little -- traded for cigarettes with a Russian that he made out of airplane parts. Like a cigarette case with Nuremberg on one side and Moscow on the other side. I'll show it to you later. And, from there when Patton started coming close to Nuremburg they marched us out. And, we marched out into Moosburg and that's where they kept us. Finally when Patton come in and were at one of the conventions and there was a 'G' man giving us a speech there he was in the lead tank coming into Moosburg. He said they had information that they were going to knock -- Hitler gave an order to knock off all POW's -- I mean -- to shoot them. And they were racing, he said Patton gave them an order to liberate that camp, which they did. They come in -- I mean -- they were still finding them. We were in the middle of a battle -- shells going over you -- which way we didn't know coming through there. They finally come into the camp, old Patton come in the next day riding with his white pistols -- you know -- in a jeep. And, we were all very happy, to see them -- you know -- from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did Patton speak at all to the prisoners when he got there?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: He may have said something there -- you know -- I mean, riding around in a jeep. I didn't hear him -- you know -- he may have talked to the officers -- cause we were both enlisted and officers in the camp. But, he was -- well, he was quite the hero. So we stayed there till they had taken us out of there they were flying everybody else out. We'd go into town and see what we can get. And there was GIs there that were -- you know -- working with Patton and went in -- had them sitting in one of the building there -- and I come up to them and they say, hay you a POW you want something to eat? Yea, come on in. Here, they had stacks of eggs in the room and he said fry him up a dozen. And I said, no way can I eat a dozen eggs -- you know -- I haven't eaten for a long time. But they were really interesting cause they were the ground solider --you know -- infantry and it was a different fighting than we did -- you know. But, they were very friendly to us and finally they flew us back into Reims, France and stayed there for a while. While they fattened us up -- you know -- feeding us milkshakes and I -- oh, and another thing in the camp. I was sitting there and this GI come in and he was looking for some sergeant, and I'm looking at him, and I said Joe -- he's my neighbor from the my old neighborhood. And the first thing Joe said is, what are doing here? Which was -- we talked for awhile. He says he was caught in the Bulge, picked up -- you know -- in the Bulge -- so he wasn't a prisoner too long. But, here you meet a next door neighbor -- you know -- which is quite a thing. Then they sent us to Camp Lucky Strike and, sailed home and -- and I guess that was history -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: It was strange because when I left I had a younger sister -- which was about fifteen years younger than I was. And she was a little toddler -- you know -- and she was a grown gal -- you know. It, it you kind of missed that in-between -- you know. My gosh, it seems strange -- you know -- that you don't have the memory of her growing up. But, it was a good reunion -- you know -- I mean -- happy. I can imagine what a pressure this must have been on my mother -- you know -- I mean -- being a prisoner, be missing. The thing was that, when I was shot down they didn't know where I was at until about September -- six, seven months after I was shot down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What date -- do you remember the date you were shot down? The date?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: April 12th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: April 12th of '44?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: '44, yes. But, they got a letter from me and they had a note they sent it to the government and that's when they got a reply that I'm a prisoner of war. I mean -- I don't believe that they had a record of it, or whatnot. It was -- you know -- inquiring about sending a package or something. Then finally she says they got a telegram stating that I'm a prisoner of war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the whole time they just knew that you were missing in action?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Missing in action. They didn't know whether I was alive or what -- you know -- until about September when they got that first e-mail or, not e-mail.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not e-mail, right, yea.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: But...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get many letters or packages, parcels in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. We didn't get anything from home and Red Cross parcels were very scarce. We're -- they keep telling us they were bombed, but I think they were pilfered -- you know. Cause we went -- oh -- quite a few months before we started getting parcels. We were getting one parcel for two prisoners and you split a parcel. But, when we moved out they gave everybody a parcel to take with them, but how can you carry it -- you know. Some of the camp that were left behind -- they marched out of their camp. They marched them around Germany for 800 miles, just didn't know where to put them. When the Germans came close they moved the other way, when the Americans or the British they moved them back. I mean -- they were just hostages -- you know. None of the prison camps would take them because they were full. So, I was fortunate in that I was moved out on a boxcar into Nuremburg.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were in Stalag -- was that Luft -- Stalag Luft 4?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. Stalag Luft 4.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Until what -- January, February of '45 -- something like that?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Uh, yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then you went to Nuremburg and then to Stalag 7A?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: 7A, yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you probably weren't at 7A very long, you don't think, before you were liberated?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. After that, it was just matter of months -- you know -- once -- once you're over -- into the new year so, must have been after December -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You went to these --

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Went to these other camps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- other places? Were you able to do much to pass the time? Somehow entertain yourselves ___?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, in camp we put -- we put on plays -- you know. Some of the guys were very talented, and we had some good chuckles in that. And, you had your bridge clubs, played cards, you walk around the compound, and you sun yourself -- and, there wasn't -- read what little books we did have. I mean -- being a new camp it -- I mean -- some of the older camps they had more entertainment that we did. But, it's mostly socializing, talking -- they had an old Victrola, which they had pass around. So, each barracks would have it every night and we'd have one guy kind of play the records, you know, the old songs and -- while we were -- cause it was lights, and that was entertaining. But, there were some classes, I guess, that people had whether you joined in or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When your plane was shot down did you lose anybody from the plane, or did everybody get out?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Everybody got out, except the radioman was the only one that lost his leg -- you know -- he was...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Lost his leg in that.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: He got hit, and he was the only one that was really damaged, you know. Well, if we would the bailed out on the first call we would have all gotten away cause they happened to land -- the four of them there they never were captured.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they're the ones who bailed out first and they were able to get in with the resistance?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Right. Yea. Well, they were there -- you know -- since I talk with the -- in corresponding with this fellow in Belgium, he tells me there was a couple, they were watching our action from their castle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: He says -- he says from their rooftop saw the planes come down. And, they verified that two planes come down. And, one they said the pilot went right straight down and crashed. The second one -- he said, the German pilot, he was shot down twice that week. And, he said he wasn't shot down, he hit the other airplane or they run into one another. And, he said, he was big liar. So, whether I got these two -- I -- I mean, it's confirmed two come down anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So. They did verify that the two --

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Verified that two were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- were shot down.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: That two were shot down. But, one of the waste gunners, Taliver (ph) wrote to my family after the war -- or, they got back before I did. And, he -- he said he saw the German planes go down. He stood right below where they parachuting down. The one went down he definitely was writing to just to my folks -- I mean -- I didn't even know this. He was writing about the action at the time we were shot down. And, he was telling them, if I write, you could tell them that Tallie (ph) called because they didn't want the information to get back to Germany they were home. I guess they put a hold on you whatever you can talk about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, do you remember your first combat mission?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, that was an easy one. We went over (?Potty de Calais?) Right over to France. We were bombing the rocket sites -- the V2 installations. So that was a -- real -- a milk run we called it. So which -- just over into France and back. And it was -- you know -- a nice easy one. Which, helps you brake into the ice -- once you went the first time, you were a veteran -- you know -- of bombing raids. Then I had the...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions in there before that 16th?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, we had -- we had one I really -- really liked. We went down to Switzerland, right on the Lake Constance, and that was a long haul. And we had a couple of airplanes go over into Switzerland. Now, everybody on that raid was going -- we were bombing right on the front and as you made your turn Switzerland was over -- everybody's on the intercom, " straight ahead, straight ahead, let's go to Switzerland", which we didn't. But, we had a few planes with feathered props that were hit -- you know -- we were going over...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And, so they landed in Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Apparently so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were just stuck there, right?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. They were interned there, probably for the rest of the war. Unless there's a way of sneaking them out of the country -- you know. But, then we had one into Torres, France, we were hitting an airfield, here that had -- must have been a lot of student pilots for the Germans and we caught those guys in the air. And, the fighters had a field day with those guys -- I mean -- being probably not experienced pilots in training and we really blasted the airfield. And -- and we saw all these fighters knocking on these poor little guys. Then one of the -- one of the raids coming back we come back with a P-38 had his tail end shot off, and he snuggled right in to our formation and we brought him all the way out of Germany to the coast and once he got over the Channel he gave us a wing -- you know -- wiggled his wings and took off -- but, he was probably happy to get back -- you know -- with our protection. Then we had an incident over our airfield when two air bombers collided and they come down right on -- right on our airfield. Missing our dump, our ammo dump, but that was another thing we'd -- England had fog. Or that -- you would take off and maybe you'd have 100 feet of clear visibility. Then you'd have 8,000 feet of just right in the cloud -- you don't see a thing. That would scare the daylights out of me cause there was 800, 900 airplanes forming above the clouds -- you know -- boy, you would break through, and boy, what a sigh of relief. Cause you didn't know who was climbing in the -- in the clouds and you couldn't see out the front window. And you'd break through and you see all these ships forming up there and you had your -- each squadron had a different marking on their forming ship and you'd form on him. You'd form your formations then you start out over the Channel. Of course -- I guess -- other people probably have better stories than I to tell.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies in the -- in the squadron, the crew, or...

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Oh yea. We were all very tight, matter of fact, we got together after the war. Mostly enlisted men -- some of the guys couldn't make it. And, we kept in touch, still do. And this Norm Bussle (ph) I met in prison camp we became good friends. Matter of fact, he's president of the Foundation -- the POW Foundation. He's from New York. And -- and you go to these conventions and you meet all your old buddies -- you know -- and stories get better every year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. We never were assigned a ship. You know -- we were replacements.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Different -- different planes?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. We'd go up and -- but the...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about a good luck charm? Did you ever have a good luck charm when you flew?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. The only thing I did when -- I had -- my job was when we would go up as engineer I'd transfer fuel -- and I would take the pins out of the bombs because they weren't armed. And, I would take those pins out and they had a little tag on them and I would save them. And, when I come back from a raid I would pin one over my bunk. And if we got shrapnel I'd hang a piece of shrapnel on it, and tie it on there. And, I had them lined up, I don't know what happened to them once we were shot down -- you know -- somebody must have picked them up. Also, I had I used to keep a log on -- on where we went, what the mission was like -- I mean -- I was writing this and they -- they ripped it all out of my logbook -- you know. When I was shot whoever picked up our clothes and stuff -- and that never came back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any targets that you really did dread going after?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Berlin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea. How many times did you fly --

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: We went twice. But, the only thing was that they could get 800 guns on you at one time -- you know -- really harm and -- and the only thing I hated -- I hated was when Dolittle (ph) come there. And, he wasn't interested in protecting the bombers. He was interested in knocking out the fighters, which, coming up to D-Day he knew more than we did-- but, we -- they would come up and they would sit way up to the side, you know, waiting for the German fighters to come up. And, he would send us in over Hannover, Brenium, and you're right in -- and you're right down Flak Alley. I mean -- if I was flying I would go some other way and detour. But he -- and right over fighters -- you know -- you can get 300 fighters. (here) A fighters and that was all he was interested in at the end. Of course, that was a prelude to D-Day where they were taking control of the skies -- I mean -- he knew what he was doing. But, it wasn't to our satisfaction.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't know if I've ask this in the while, describe a typical day of a mission. You know -- what time did you get up, and how did that go?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, you'd get somebody would come around and tapping you on the head -- hay, you're up -- you know -- wake up man. You get up, clean up, wash. You go down for breakfast. If you were hungry or -- you know -- and then you'd go down to -- to briefing. And, they would sit there and wait for them to raise the screen on the mission board -- where the string-- where you were going. Well, if it was deep into Germany you'd hear a lot of oohs and ahs -- where we going. Oh boy, and you'd be going and then after that why'd you'd go down to pick up your flight gear, your parachute, your -- they'd give you these packets for your escape kits. And, of course our -- our pilot he would grab us all and go down to the Chaplain and before every raid we's have to sit there and get a group prayer with us -- which was nice. Old, Herb Shultz (ph)he -- and then get together, then you wait for transportation out to your plane -- and you go. Everybody went out to the different planes and you get in there and you check that out -- you know -- your guns -- make sure you had ammo and whatnot. And then you'd -- everybody get in there waiting for the start. You'd start up and then you'd lineup behind one another on the runways prior to take off. And, you approached -- you know -- takeoff while you're a couple of minutes behind the guy in front of you in taking off. You'd sit there and I would have to check the ailerons with the pilot you need to call out right, left and make a visual inspection. And that used to be interesting seeing all those airplanes lined-up -- you know -- taking off like taxi cabs at a curb -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind when you think about those years?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: They were good years -- you know. It was the funniest thing -- I wasn't scare or -- when I went on these raids. I mean -- your thought was never one of fear. Even in the last day when we had that gun battle there -- I mean -- shooting at the plane. I wasn't thinking of myself -- you know -- it was get that guy -- shoot that plane down. Well, is wasn't the man it was the plane. You weren't killing a person you were knocking down a vehicle. So, it wasn't -- once on the ground that's a different story. Then it sets in -- you know -- you're -- here am I -- where am I -- and you're bleeding a little bit -- you know -- you got wounds, you got burns. But, the I think the worse part of it was when you landed on the ground and you wondering -- where am I -- you know -- what am I going to do now? And it's that uncertainty -- you know -- you never figured it's going to be me, it's always going to be the other guy. Well, I don't know if -- anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else? You got some stuff here to show me?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. I got these -- well, now this Kane (ph) he -- that's him -- he was a German from Wisconsin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: But, the guys were telling me they were in the house in Belgium up -- upstairs and they had a window overlooking the outside. And he was always kind of a -- liked to drink and -- you know -- play around. He said they're standing up there in the window and a couple of Belgium girls walk by and he starts whistling for them and other guys said we nearly killed him. He said, give away our hideout -- you know -- they had them up in an attic. And -- and he thought he was back in America you know. He was one a (be)-- this was one of the - one of the resistance. He wrote a book about his experience and I don't know how he got my picture in there -- in his book. He wrote that he said he got my whole name he had Wargo instead of Vargo.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: But, that's -- that's the picture that they would give you to take with you in your escape kit. And the only thing bad about that every tenth guy would have the same shirt, the same tie.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where did he get that picture? You don't know?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I had that in my escape kit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh. So he took it out of the escape kit? Or you--

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I gave it to him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You gave it to him before you were taken by the--

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well you would give it to them and they had make these -- if you needed identification papers --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: -- and whatnot. So we marched -- I enjoyed that march out of Nuremburg because you were kind of free to roam --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: -- to the certain degree. And the march we'd be able to steal potatoes or whatever food we could get. And I remember one night -- it was real raining day and we were sleeping in the woods and in the morning nobody would move and the Germans kept hollering at us to come out then -- then finally they took a machine gun and sprayed the top of the trees making us come out. So, we come out there and we were strafed while we were marching. Two P47s come down on our column they must have thought we were Germans marching we were in ___ an boy did we hit the dirt in the ditches on the side. The next day we had big POW signs -- you know -- on our -- on our march out of there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they get anybody?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I don't know if anybody was hurt -- I mean -- the column was long and you really didn't know, they may have hit somebody -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I know a lot -- a couple of guys took off -- you know -- while we were marching. Course they had orders that said do not try to escape because they were right behind us were the SS. I mean -- they were the real echelon and they said they wouldn't take prisoners. They would just as soon shoot you -- you know. But, they were holding back -- I guess -- Patton's Army -- you know -- and then they disappeared over the hill cause once Patton come to the camp -- there was sort of a river there -- they had artillery barrages back and forth. And they come in and tanks went ahead and cleared that out -- I guess. And another thing was when they liberated the camp they brought in bread -- white bread -- and it tasted like Angle Food Cake. And I said, " Boy, this is cake we were so used to that sawdust and black bread. And, this neighbor of mine, that was prisoner, his son was in the service. He went over to see him after the war -- he brought back a loaf of black bread. He said, "I thought you'd miss this." I said, "Thanks Joe, that's just what I want."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they still making it out of same stuff at that point?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. I doubt it. It -- it was a dark German rye of some kind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly --

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: But just as fun -- you know -- something to remind me of the old days -- yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't put the sawdust in any more.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No -- they -- yea, that bread would turn moldy and whatnot. That was -- then we had a Christmas, our first Christmas in a -- in a Stalag 4 and we finally got Red Cross parcels. And everybody was trying to cook up something -- I mean -- I guess -- the thought of home and Christmas cooking. But everybody was trying to concock (ph) something out of what they had -- you know -- your plums, your prunes, or your crackers. I -- it was surprising we didn't all die. What they were trying to make -- you know. But, we had a real nice Christmas. We pooled all our food -- you know -- sang songs that night. I think they -- think they let us out of the compound to let us walk around. And it was so nice, you know, being out under the stars and out of the compound at night. So, that was one of the nicest days -- this Norm, he -- he remembers that too. He called -- said, you remember at Christmas time -- he said, "You remember that Christmas?" -- I said, "sure do." Yep -- well, you kind of form a buddy-buddy relationship with your POWs -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: You got a kind of a feeling for them -- you know what they been through -- you know. They don't have to tell you -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned the Angle Food taste?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was exactly what -- the words my dad used to describe it when he got the bread.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: He did?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He said that's exactly what he said when he first tasted white bread, it tasted like Angel Food cake.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: It was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, obviously it had that sensation for a lot of guys.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. It -- it well -- I mean -- when they threw those loaves at us -- well, you couldn't eat too much at the time -- you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: But, they got back to Rheims, France and they -- they were well, taking care of us -- giving us call them high milkshakes, or potent drinks of -- build up your muscles -- you know -- your weight. Where was your dad at?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was held in Lindberg for a while -- a short while. And then -- I can't remember now. But, then he ended up in Stalag 4C in Czechoslovakia.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Oh, yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And he was on a labor detail there.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea. That's -- he was there for about four months until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: That's something we didn't have to do was work.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea. Well, he thought -- you know -- it was -- I don't know if anyone had to work. But, they came around to the camp in Lindberg and asked for volunteers. And, they said if you do this you'll get more food. And so my Dad thought this was the only way he could survive so he volunteered to do it and there wasn't much more food.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. I would of gone out too, really just to get out of the camp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Sure.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: You know. Get out, and some guys even worked on some were farms, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: They had them doing some farm work -- which would -- you'd had done anything to get out of the camp there. When you're locked up -- I mean -- it's limited in what you can do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I mean, even though there's activities, but trying to get out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, that's about...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think we got it?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Well, that's about it -- you know -- there was a story here forget about. These two Belgium boys one day after the war wrote a letter to the Mayor of Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh hum.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: And looking for me.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Bergermeister (ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really? And to the Bergermeister.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: To the Bergermeister. About Nicholas Vargo, and I was at down at Dayton at Wright-Patterson at the time. And, they come down there looking for me. They translated the...

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: It was written in French, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. In French. And this is the Mr. Mayor letter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It is an account of one of your inhabits of your community.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea. Just like a little village or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he's got this letter, actually it's your 16th mission, right?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Although he says 15th raid on Germany so maybe...

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: That was that your 15 mission?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Either 15th or 16th.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Well, it was two days after Easter that year; that's all I know.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea cause...

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Did you -- you had completed three fives, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So yea, if you've got the --

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I got the air medals for two clusters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Air medals for each five, right?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea, exactly. If it's two clusters then you must have completed 15.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yea. I think it was the 16th.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Because I -- I had pulled one extra mission with a -- as a replacement on some other crew -- you know -- you'd be up there every morning in case somebody was sick or something -- I know, I went on one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who was the mayor at this time?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Was it one who got his hair burnt?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: The mayor.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Oh, what the heck was his name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when was this written? Right at the end of the war? Right after the war?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Right after the war, yea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Can't even think of the man's...

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: It's 1945, must be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 1945 -- October 45.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: The Mayor of Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's just to the Mayor of Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: He must have figured, like the little villages.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. In Belgium, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You end up forgetting--

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: You know -- you talk to the Bergermeister, he knows everything -- you know. And, they come chase me down at...

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Wright Field (ph).

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Wright Field. It was one of those.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in the reserves then at Wright Field?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: No. I was still in service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still in service -- oh, you hadn't been discharged yet?

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: I was working down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Nicholas S. Vargo
sp.p: Some guy by the name of Folley (ph) interpreted or...
